Patient Vignette: Tui, Age 30

Tui arrives for her sessions still in her work pants, the knees stained with copper dust and pipe sealant, a faint smell of solder clinging to her flannel shirt. She is a plumber, the only woman on her crew, and she tells me she likes the work because it is straightforward-when a pipe is broken, you fix it. There is no ambiguity. She has been married for six years to a man named Matt, who works as a high school science teacher. She describes him as "patient," but when she says the word, her jaw tightens.

The story she tells begins not in a single moment, but in a texture. She grew up in a small coastal town in Oceania, the eldest of four children. Her father was a fisherman, a man who was loved in the community for his generosity and his laugh. At home, that laugh could turn into a roar in the space of a breath. She does not remember the first time he hit her. She remembers the pattern: a wrong word, a dish left in the sink, a grade that was not good enough. He would use his belt, or his open hand, or the wooden spoon. Her mother would look away, would busy herself with the kettle, would say later, "He works so hard. He doesn't mean it."

Tui learned to read the air. She learned to walk softly, to make herself small, to anticipate the shift in his breathing that meant the storm was coming. She learned that safety was a lie.

When she was fourteen, she broke her arm trying to stop him from hitting her younger brother. She told the emergency room doctor she fell off her bike. She remembers the way the doctor looked at her father, the way her father smiled and shook his head, saying, "Clumsy girl." The doctor did not ask again. Tui learned that adults would not help.

She left home at seventeen, moving to the city for a trade school program. She chose plumbing because it was physical, because it required tools, because no one would tell her she was too soft. She was good at it. She met Matt in her mid-twenties, and she was careful with him at first, waiting for the switch to flip. It never did. He is gentle. He asks before he touches her. He does not raise his voice.

But Tui lives in a body that does not believe in safety.

In session, she describes a recurring experience that happens at work. She will be under a sink, the light dim, the space tight, and a male coworker will call her name from the other room. If his tone is too loud, or too sudden, her vision goes white. She feels a cold sweat break out on her neck. Her hands shake so badly she cannot hold a wrench. She has to crawl out, sit on the tailgate of the truck, and stare at the sky until her heart stops pounding. She tells the crew she is "checking the inventory." They believe her. She is grateful for the lie.

At home, she sleeps on the edge of the bed, always facing the door. She has a nightmare that repeats: she is a child again, standing in the kitchen, and her father is walking toward her. But in the dream, she is an adult, and she has a pipe wrench in her hand. She wants to swing it. She cannot move. She wakes up with her teeth clenched, her jaw aching.

Matt has learned not to touch her when she is asleep. Once, he put a hand on her shoulder to wake her from a nightmare, and she punched him in the chest. She cried for an hour afterward. He said it was okay. She does not believe him.

She avoids her hometown. She has not spoken to her father in six years. She sends her mother a birthday card every year, but she does not write a return address. She says she is not angry-she says it flatly, like a fact, like the pressure in a pipe that has been shut off for so long the valve is rusted shut.

On her PCL-5, she scored a 34. She endorsed feeling distant from people, having trouble sleeping, and being constantly on guard. She marked "moderately" for the question about avoiding memories. She told me she does not think about the past. She thinks about the job. She thinks about the next pipe, the next fitting, the next simple problem she can solve with her hands.

But her hands are shaking. And she does not know why.
